identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Tulja Bhavani Temple is counted among the 51 Shakti Pithas and, together with Renuka (Mahur), Mahalakshmi (Kolhapur) and Saptashringi (Vani), is regarded as one of four principal Shakti shrines of Maharashtra. The goddess Bhavani here is worshipped as a manifestation of Parvati/Durga, and the temple is closely associated in tradition with Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, whose family is said to have been devotees of the deity.

narrative.summaryIntro:
Tulja Bhavani Temple stands in the town of Tuljapur in Dharashiv (formerly Osmanabad) district of Maharashtra, on the Yamunachala hill of the Balaghat range. Dedicated to the goddess Bhavani, it is one of the 51 Shakti Pithas of the subcontinent and is counted among the four principal Shakti shrines of Maharashtra, alongside the temples at Mahur, Kolhapur and Vani.

The temple is built of black stone in the Hemadpanti architectural idiom associated with the medieval Deccan. It draws very large numbers of pilgrims through the year, with the heaviest crowds during the Sharadiya Navaratri festival in the Hindu month of Ashwin. The site is closely tied in regional tradition to the Bhonsle family and to Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, who is said to have been a devotee of the goddess; two of the temple's entrance gates are named after his parents, Shahaji and Jijabai.
narrative.documentedHistory:
Wikipedia dates the temple's founding to the 12th century CE, traditionally to 1169, attributing it to Mahamandaleshwara Māradadeva of the Kadamb dynasty. The temple sits at approximately 18°00′41″N 76°07′32″E at an elevation of about 648 m, on the Yamunachala hill of the Balaghat range near the Mandakini river and the Bori dam, about 45 km northeast of Solapur. The structure is built of black stone in the Hemadpanti style.

The temple's association with Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj is presented in sourced material as regional tradition rather than as independently documented history: Wikipedia states he was "reputed to frequently visit this temple to seek blessings," and that two of the temple's entrances are named after his parents, Shahaji and Jijabai. No source opened for this record documents a specific sword-gifting episode, so that narrative is not restated here.

Governance of the temple is described somewhat differently across sources. The temple's own trust website states the temple was registered as a public trust in 1962 under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, and that its operations follow "Kawayat Deval" rules dating to the Nizam's administration. Wikipedia separately states that day-to-day affairs are overseen by a trust headed by the District Collector, while the Government of India's utsav.gov.in tourism portal describes management and priestly rights as resting with the Kadamb Bhope family, descendants of the temple's traditional founder, through an organisation it names Shri Tuljabhavani Mandir Sansthan. These descriptions are not necessarily contradictory — a registered public trust, government oversight through the District Collector, and hereditary priestly rights can coexist — but no single source opened for this record reconciles all three, so all three are reported here rather than resolved into one.

Wikipedia also reports a large corridor redevelopment project for the temple precinct, budgeted at approximately ₹1,865 crore and targeted for completion by December 2028, as of the article's most recent update.

editorial.verificationNotes: Contact details, poojas and festival names are sourced to the temple trust's own website (official temple source). Darshan timings come from the Government of India's utsav.gov.in tourism portal (government source) rather than from the trust site itself, whose own 'Hours' field (10:00 AM–6:00 PM) appears to describe office/administrative hours rather than darshan hours and was not used for openingHours. History, architecture and the Shivaji-era tradition rely on Wikipedia (tertiary, non-official) and are marked accordingly. Multiple third-party pilgrimage-guide sites give conflicting darshan hours (e.g. 4:00 AM–10:00 PM); none of those pages were opened directly and none is cited here.

visitingInfo.nearestBusStation: Tuljapur is well connected by road to Solapur (approx. 45 km) and Dharashiv/Osmanabad town (approx. 25 km)
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Confirm current darshan hours, VIP/Sinhasan pooja booking and festival-day arrangements with the temple trust before travelling. Trust phone: +91 9422956830 / +91 9067257215; email shrituljabhavanitemple@gmail.com. Address: Mahadwar Road, Tuljapur, Dharashiv District, Maharashtra 413601.

openingHours.notes: Timing as published on the Government of India's utsav.gov.in tourism portal. The temple trust's own website lists a separate 10:00 AM–6:00 PM 'Hours' field that appears to be office/administrative hours rather than darshan hours; that figure is not used here. Timings are known to extend or change during Navaratri and other festivals.

shrines.locationDescription: One of the temple's entrance gates; named, per Wikipedia, after Shivaji Maharaj's father Shahaji Bhonsle.
A second temple entrance gate named, per Wikipedia, after Shivaji Maharaj's mother Jijabai.

poojas.description: Daily morning abhishekam performed with milk provided through the Chhatrapati Kolhapur Institution, per the temple trust's website.
Daily evening abhishekam, per the temple trust's website.

A booked pooja using an offering of roughly 70 litres of materials including yogurt, milk, condensed milk and mango or sugarcane juice; the trust website states it is performed across five sessions in the morning and two in the evening, without giving exact clock times.

festivals.significance: The temple's principal annual festival, a nine-day celebration culminating in Vijayadashami (Dussehra); draws the temple's largest crowds of the year.
Described by the temple trust as a mirror celebration of the Sharadiya Navaratri, observed roughly three months later.
Listed by Wikipedia among festivals observed at the temple, alongside Navaratri and Dussehra.
